title: Design Strategies
description: Six design strategies — linear, iterative, inclusive, user-centred, sustainable and ergonomic — their contexts.
content_html:
What Is a Design Strategy?

A design strategy is the overarching approach a designer chooses before any sketching or modelling begins. The strategy shapes every decision that follows: how much time is spent on research, whether users are consulted, and how many times the design is revised. OCR R038 requires you to know six named strategies, understand when each suits a project, and weigh up the advantages and disadvantages of each.

Linear Design

Linear design follows a step-by-step sequence: analyse the brief, research, write a specification, generate ideas, make a prototype, then evaluate. Each stage is completed before the next begins, and the process does not loop back. This approach suits projects with a very clear, stable brief — for example, manufacturing a replacement component to an agreed technical standard where the requirements are already fully known.

The main advantage of linear design is its predictability: timelines and budgets are easier to plan because the scope is fixed. The disadvantage is inflexibility — if a problem is discovered late in the process (say, during manufacture) there is no formal mechanism to revise the design, which can be costly.

Key Fact

The six design strategies you must know for R038 are: linear, iterative, inclusive, user-centred, sustainable, and ergonomic design. Questions may ask you to recommend one strategy for a given context and justify your choice — always name the strategy precisely and then explain why it fits that scenario.

Iterative Design

Iterative design is a cyclic process: the designer produces an idea, tests or evaluates it, identifies weaknesses, then redesigns and tests again. Each loop refines the product. This strategy suits complex or novel products where requirements are not fully understood at the start — consumer electronics, medical devices and bespoke engineering solutions all benefit from an iterative approach.

The advantage of iterative design is that problems are caught early and the product is progressively improved to better meet the brief. The disadvantage is that the process can be time-consuming and expensive if many revision cycles are needed, and it requires clear decision criteria for when to stop iterating.

Inclusive Design

Inclusive design aims to create products that can be used by the widest possible range of people, regardless of age, ability or background — without the need for specialist adaptation. A classic engineering example is the OXO Good Grips peeler, designed so that people with limited grip strength (including those with arthritis) can use it as easily as anyone else. Inclusive design suits products that will be used in public spaces or by diverse populations.

The advantage is that an inclusive product reaches a larger market and avoids the need for costly specialist versions. The disadvantage is that designing for the full range of users can add complexity and cost to the development process, and may mean compromising on optimisation for any one group.

User-centred design (UCD) places the needs, preferences and limitations of the end user at the centre of every design decision. Designers gather detailed user research — through interviews, observation and testing — and continually involve users throughout the process. UCD suits consumer products where user experience is critical, such as smartphone interfaces, hospital equipment or workplace tools. The advantage is that the final product is highly likely to meet real user needs, reducing the chance of market failure. The disadvantage is that extensive user research and testing adds time and cost, and user feedback can sometimes conflict or be difficult to interpret.

Sustainable Design

Sustainable design considers the environmental impact of a product across its entire lifecycle — from raw material extraction through manufacture, use and eventual disposal. Designers using this strategy might choose recycled materials, minimise energy use in manufacture, or design for disassembly so components can be reused. It suits any product where environmental credentials are a key market requirement — from packaging to renewable energy hardware.

The advantage of sustainable design is reduced environmental impact and, increasingly, commercial appeal as consumers prioritise green credentials. The disadvantage is that sustainable materials and processes can cost more, and life-cycle analysis adds complexity to the design process.

Key Fact

Linear design is the only strategy that does not include a formal feedback loop — all other strategies involve some form of review or refinement. This distinction is important: exam questions frequently ask you to explain why a company chose an iterative rather than a linear approach, or vice versa.

Ergonomic Design

Ergonomic design optimises the interaction between a product and the human body — considering posture, reach, force, comfort and safety. Engineers use anthropometric data (measurements of human body dimensions) to ensure products fit the range of users. Ergonomic design is essential for tools, workstations, vehicles and any equipment used repeatedly over long periods, where poor fit leads to injury or error.

The advantage of ergonomic design is improved user safety and comfort, which reduces injury rates and increases productivity. The disadvantage is that designing for the full range of body sizes requires detailed anthropometric research, and it may not always be possible to satisfy every user simultaneously — some products are designed for the 5th to 95th percentile range, which still excludes a small proportion of users.

Exam questions will often give you a design scenario and ask which strategy would be most appropriate. Use this logic: if the brief is fixed and the product is a known type (e.g. replacing a standard bracket), linear design is efficient. If the product is novel or complex, iterative design allows refinement. If the product must serve diverse or less-abled users, consider inclusive or user-centred design. If the client specifically requires low environmental impact, sustainable design is the priority. If the product is worn or handled repeatedly and must fit the human body well, ergonomic design takes precedence. A strong answer will name the strategy, describe its key feature, and link it directly to the scenario — never just list strategies without explanation.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to "recommend a design strategy" for a scenario, name the strategy precisely (use the exact term from the spec) and then justify your choice with at least two reasons linked to the scenario. Vague answers such as "they should use a good strategy" score zero. For "advantages and disadvantages" questions, give a specific advantage and a specific disadvantage — do not simply state that one strategy is "better" than another without explaining why in context.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The six design strategies are linear, iterative, inclusive, user-centred, sustainable and ergonomic — each suits a different context, and you must know when to recommend each one and be able to state at least one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
  • Linear design is the only strategy without a feedback loop; iterative design is explicitly cyclic and is used when requirements evolve during development.
  • Ergonomic design relies on anthropometric data to match products to the human body, while inclusive design broadens usability for the widest possible range of people — these two strategies are related but distinct.

glossary_terms.definition: A structured approach that guides how a designer or engineering team tackles a design problem from brief to final product.
A design strategy that moves through a fixed sequence of stages — brief, research, specification, design, make, evaluate — without returning to earlier stages.
A cyclical design strategy in which the designer repeatedly designs, makes, evaluates and improves a product through successive cycles until requirements are met.
Statistical data about the dimensions of the human body, used to ensure products fit the range of people who will use them.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the linear design strategy?
A) A cyclic process that repeats until the product meets the specification
B) A step-by-step sequence that does not loop back to earlier stages
C) A process that places the user at the centre of every design decision
D) An approach that considers the environmental impact of the whole product lifecycle
practice_questions.marks: B) A step-by-step sequence that does not loop back to earlier stages [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two design strategies that would be suitable when designing a product intended to be used by people of all ages and abilities.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: inclusive design / user-centred design (accept either or both). Accept ergonomic design with a valid brief justification. Do not accept vague answers such as 'a good strategy' with no named strategy. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of using an iterative design strategy rather than a linear design strategy when developing a new type of medical monitoring device.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant advantage (e.g. 'the design can be improved through repeated cycles'). 2 marks for development (e.g. 'problems discovered during testing can be fed back into the design, so errors are corrected before manufacture'). 3 marks for a fully developed explanation applied to the medical device context (e.g. 'because a medical device must be highly reliable and its requirements may not be fully known at the start, iterative cycles of testing and refinement allow the team to discover and fix faults progressively, reducing the risk of producing a device that fails in clinical use'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the ergonomic design strategy. Give one example of a product where this strategy would be particularly appropriate and explain why.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): ergonomic design optimises the fit between a product and the human body, using anthropometric data about body dimensions to ensure comfort, safety and efficient use (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement mentioning the human body or anthropometrics).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, an office chair — the seat height, back support angle and armrest position must match a wide range of user body dimensions so that workers can sit safely for extended periods without developing musculoskeletal strain (2 marks for a specific, well-explained example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
An engineering company is designing a new public water fountain intended for installation in a city park. The fountain will be used by adults, children, wheelchair users and people with visual impairments.

Discuss which design strategy or strategies would be most appropriate for this project.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion identifying at least two appropriate strategies (e.g. inclusive design to serve diverse users including wheelchair users and visually impaired people; user-centred design to involve users in testing; ergonomic design to ensure correct operating heights and reach). Each strategy is explained with reasons linked to the scenario, with comparison of their relative suitability. Both the strengths of the recommended approach and the challenges or limitations are addressed.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant strategies identified and explained with some reference to the fountain scenario, but without full comparison or discussion of limitations.
Developing (2 marks): One relevant strategy identified and briefly explained, or two strategies named without development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development or no named strategy. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer is deciding whether to use a linear or iterative design strategy to develop a completely new type of electric bicycle that incorporates several untested technologies.

Evaluate which design strategy would be more appropriate for this project. Use your knowledge of both strategies to support your judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that clearly explains the key features of both linear and iterative design, argues persuasively for iterative design given the novelty and technical uncertainty of the product, and addresses the counter-argument (linear design is cheaper and faster if requirements are well-defined — but they are not here). The answer reaches a clear, reasoned judgement with evidence from the scenario (untested technologies, need for repeated testing and refinement). Quality of written communication is high and terminology is precise.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both strategies described accurately, at least two reasons given for preferring iterative design applied to the scenario, and an attempt at a judgement, but the counter-argument may be underdeveloped.
Developing (3–4 marks): One or both strategies described, some relevant reasoning, but largely one-sided or without a clear evaluative judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic description of one strategy with little or no comparison or application to the electric bicycle scenario. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which design strategy specifically uses a cyclic process of designing, making and evaluating before returning to the design stage?
Which design strategy aims to create products usable by the widest possible range of people, without the need for specialist adaptation?
Ergonomic design uses _____ — statistical data about human body dimensions — to ensure a product fits the range of intended users.
Linear design is the only strategy that does not include a _____ — meaning problems found late in the process cannot be formally addressed without restarting.
Match each design strategy to the context in which it is most appropriate.
right: The brief is fixed and requirements are fully known from the start
Reducing environmental impact across the whole product lifecycle is the key client requirement
The end user's needs, preferences and limitations must drive every design decision

flashcard_questions.q: What are the six design strategies you must know for OCR R038?
flashcard_questions.a: The six design strategies are linear design, iterative design, inclusive design, user-centred design, sustainable design, and ergonomic design.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key feature that distinguishes linear design from all other strategies?
flashcard_questions.a: Linear design follows a fixed, sequential set of stages and does not include a feedback loop, so it cannot formally return to earlier stages once they are complete.

flashcard_questions.q: What is iterative design and when does it suit a project best?
flashcard_questions.a: Iterative design is a cyclic strategy in which the designer repeatedly designs, tests and refines the product — it suits complex or novel projects where requirements are not fully.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the aim of inclusive design?
flashcard_questions.a: Inclusive design aims to create products that can be used by the widest possible range of people, including those with disabilities or limited mobility, without specialist adaptation.

flashcard_questions.q: How does user-centred design differ from inclusive design?
flashcard_questions.a: User-centred design places the specific needs and preferences of the intended user at the centre of all decisions through ongoing research and testing, whereas inclusive design focuses on maximising.

flashcard_questions.q: State one advantage and one disadvantage of iterative design.
flashcard_questions.a: One advantage is that problems are caught and corrected early through repeated testing cycles; one disadvantage is that the process can be more time-consuming and costly than a linear approach.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of data does ergonomic design use to match a product to its users?
flashcard_questions.a: Ergonomic design uses anthropometric data — statistical measurements of human body dimensions — to ensure the product fits the range of people who will use it.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one context in which linear design would be appropriate.
flashcard_questions.a: Linear design is appropriate when the brief is clear and stable from the start, such as manufacturing a replacement component to an agreed technical standard where all requirements are.

flashcard_questions.q: State one advantage of sustainable design.
flashcard_questions.a: A key advantage of sustainable design is that it reduces the environmental impact of the product across its whole lifecycle, from raw material extraction through to disposal.

flashcard_questions.q: State one disadvantage of inclusive design.
flashcard_questions.a: A disadvantage of inclusive design is that designing for the full range of users adds complexity and cost to the development process, and may require compromising on optimisation for.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the 5th to 95th percentile range mean in ergonomic design?
flashcard_questions.a: The 5th to 95th percentile range means the product is designed to fit the middle 90% of the population — excluding the most extreme 5% at each end.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might a company choose iterative rather than linear design for a new medical device?
flashcard_questions.a: A company would choose iterative design for a medical device because the product is novel and safety-critical, so repeated cycles of testing and refinement are needed to discover and.
